hops.afterHeading: Staying in the lane: CXCL12 and CXCR4
hops.title: A shelved HIV drug that frees stem cells from bone marrow
hops.text: Plerixafor began as an HIV project. A chemical impurity pointed chemists to a family of compounds, which they refined into AMD3100, an anti-HIV agent whose target turned out to be CXCR4. In a 2000 Johns Hopkins safety study, no drug was detectable in the blood after the oral doses tested. Injected, it raised white cell counts to as much as three times baseline. A 2003 study found blood-forming CD34-positive cells up several-fold. Blocking CXCR4 had loosened the CXCL12 hold that keeps them in the marrow. In 2008 the FDA approved it, given with G-CSF, to collect patients' own stem cells for transplant in non-Hodgkin lymphoma or multiple myeloma.

sources.citation: De Clercq E, Antivir Chem Chemother 27:2040206619829382 (2019)
Hendrix CW et al., Antimicrob Agents Chemother 44:1667-1673 (2000)

image.caption: Blocking CXCR4 breaks the CXCL12 hold that keeps blood-forming stem cells in the bone marrow.

hops.title: A baby's frontal lobe is still receiving migrating interneurons
hops.text: It is easy to assume a newborn's cortex is already fully stocked with neurons. In 2016 Mercedes Paredes, Arturo Alvarez-Buylla and colleagues examined postmortem infant brains and found young neurons in a dense arch beside the lateral ventricles; MRI of living infants showed a signal of the same shape. They called it the Arc. More than ninety percent of its young neurons contained GABA, and the team also detected CXCR4 on them. Near the ventricles the cells moved sideways, some along blood vessels, then spread toward the frontal cortex. Most of this happened in the first three months after birth, and a few elongated cells remained at seven months.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A sleeping newborn baby in a sunlit wooden crib beneath a curving crescent wooden mobile.
image.caption: In human infants, young GABA-containing neurons keep travelling toward the frontal cortex for months after birth.

hops.afterHeading: The rostral migratory stream: a tangential route for life
hops.title: Dolphins cannot smell, and their adult neuron nursery is a remnant
hops.text: Dolphins descend from land mammals that could smell, yet adult dolphins have no sense of smell and no olfactory bulb. That lets researchers ask whether the region that feeds a mouse's bulb still makes neurons in an animal that has lost both. In 2017 Roberta Parolisi, Bruno Cozzi and Luca Bonfanti examined dolphin brains and found only a small leftover strip where a rodent's subventricular nursery sits. Even in newborn dolphins, it appeared to have lost its capacity to make neurons. Mice keep their rostral migratory stream running for life. The authors suggest that, in dolphins, adult neuron production there faded away along with the sense of smell.

sources.citation: Parolisi R, Cozzi B & Bonfanti L, Brain Struct Funct 222:2625-2639 (2017)
Parolisi R, Cozzi B & Bonfanti L, Front Neurosci 12:497 (2018)
